intro: An extended participial attribute (erweitertes Partizipialattribut) packs a whole relative clause between the article and the noun: die Reform, die von der Regierung geplant wird → die von der Regierung geplante Reform. Everything that belonged to the clause (agent, time, place, object) stands in front of the participle, and the participle takes an ordinary adjective ending. Partizip I (steigend, belastend) means the noun is doing something itself: die seit Jahren steigenden Mieten. Partizip II of a transitive verb is passive (die erzielten Umsätze = the sales that were achieved); of a sein-verb it is active and completed (die angekommene Delegation). zu + Partizip I is the Gerundivum and means 'must / can be done': der zu prüfende Antrag = der Antrag, der geprüft werden muss. Academic, legal and press German are full of these frames; reading them means finding the article, jumping to the noun, then reading the middle.
tips[0].title: Partizip I = active, simultaneous
tips[0].text: A relative clause in the active present becomes Partizip I (infinitive + d) with an adjective ending. The object and adverbs of the clause move in front of it.
tips[0].check.why: The children are doing the playing, so Partizip I (spielend), with the plural ending -en after die.
tips[1].title: Partizip II = passive, or completed with sein-verbs
tips[1].text: A transitive verb gives a passive meaning: die geplante Reform (is/was planned). A verb with a sein-perfect gives an active, completed meaning: die angekommene Delegation, die angetretenen Parteien.
tips[1].trap: Verbs with a haben-perfect and no accusative object have no attributive Partizip II: *die teilgenommenen Personen, *der geschlafene Gast. Use Partizip I (die teilnehmenden Personen) or another verb (die beteiligten Personen).
tips[1].check.why: teilnehmen has a haben-perfect and no accusative object, so it has no attributive Partizip II. Use Partizip I: die teilnehmenden Personen.
tips[2].title: zu + Partizip I = must / can be done
tips[2].text: The Gerundivum replaces a relative clause with müssen/können/sollen + passive, or with sein + zu. Separable verbs take zu inside the word: einzureichend-, anzuerkennend-.
tips[2].check.why: sein + zu becomes the Gerundivum zu + Partizip I, and in a separable verb zu goes inside: ab-zu-rechnend-en. abgerechneten would mean they are already settled.
tips[2].visual.rows[0].b: die Kosten, die zu erwarten sind
tips[2].visual.rows[1].b: ein Risiko, das man nicht unterschätzen darf
tips[3].title: Unpacking: article → noun → back to the middle
tips[3].text: Find the article, jump to the first noun that fits it, then build the relative clause from the words in between. A Gerundivum unpacks to sein + zu + infinitive or to a modal verb + passive.
tips[3].check.why: Article die → noun Preiserhöhungen; the middle (von der Firma angekündigt) becomes the relative clause. A plain Partizip II carries no must.
table.caption: From relative clause to participial attribute
remember[0]: Partizip I = the noun does it; Partizip II = it was done to the noun (or, with sein-verbs, the noun has done it).
remember[1]: zu + Partizip I = must / can be done; separable verbs: ein-zu-reichend.
remember[2]: The participle takes a normal adjective ending: der geplante, ein geplanter, mit den geplanten, im Ausland ausgebildeter Fachkräfte.
mistakes[0].why: teilnehmen has a haben-perfect and no accusative object, so its Partizip II cannot be used attributively.
mistakes[1].why: An ongoing process needs Partizip I; after die in the plural the ending is -en.
mistakes[2].why: With separable verbs zu goes between prefix and stem, written as one word.
mistakes[3].why: The whole attribute stands between article and noun, never after the noun.
hook: Crack the long noun phrases of newspapers and law — die seit Jahren steigenden Mieten — by reading article, noun, then the middle.
recall.known: From "Erweitertes Partizipialattribut": article … complements … participle … noun.
recall.today: zu + Partizip I: die zu erwartenden Kosten.
